Gravity acting on the mass (the amount of matter) of an object creates a force called weight. The rotor blade below weighs 100 lbs. It is 20 feet long (span) and is 1 foot wide (chord). Accordingly, its surface area is 20 square feet. [Figure 2-1]

The blade is perfectly balanced on a pinpoint stand, as you can see in Figure 2-2 from looking at it from the end (the airfoil view). The goal is for the blade to defy gravity and stay exactly where it is when we remove the stand. If we do nothing before removing the stand, the blade will simply fall to the ground. Can we exert a force (a push or pull) opposite gravity that equals the 100 lb. weight of the blade? Yes, for example, electromagnetic force could be used. In helicopters, however, we use aerodynamic force to oppose weight and to maneuver.

Every object in the atmosphere is surrounded by a gas that exerts a static force of 2,116 lb per square foot (a force times a unit area, called pressure) at sea level. However, that pressure is exerted equally all over the blade (top and bottom) and therefore does not create any useful force on the blade. We need only create a difference of a single pound of static pressure differential per square foot of blade surface to have a force equal to the blade's weight (100 lb of upward pressure opposite 100 lb downward weight).

Total pressure consists of static pressure and, if the air is moving, dynamic pressure (a pressure in the direction of the air movement). As shown in Figure 2-3, if dynamic pressure is increased the static pressure will decrease. Due to the design of the airfoil, the velocity of the air passing over the upper surface will be greater than that of the lower surface, leading to higher dynamic pressure on the upper surface than on the lower surface. The higher dynamic pressure on the upper surface lowers the static pressure on the upper surface. The static pressure on the bottom will now be greater than the static pressure on the top. The blade will experience an upward force. With just the right amount of air passing over the blade the upward force will equal one pound per square foot. This upward force is equal to, and acts opposite the blade's weight of 100 lb. So, if we now remove the stand, the blade will defy gravity and remain in its position (ignoring rearward drag for the moment).

The force created by air moving over an object (or moving an object through the air) is called aerodynamic force. Aero means air. Dynamic means moving or motion. Accordingly, by moving the air over an airfoil we can change the static pressures on the top and bottom thereby generating a useful force (an aerodynamic force). The portion of the aerodynamic force that is usually measured perpendicular to the air flowing around the airfoil is called lift and is used to oppose weight. Drag is the portion of aerodynamic force that is measured as the resistance created by an object passing through the air (or having the air passed over it). Drag acts in a streamwise direction with the wind passing over the airfoil and retards forward movement.

Forces Acting on the Aircraft

Once a helicopter leaves the ground, it is acted upon by four aerodynamic forces; thrust, drag, lift, and weight. Understanding how these forces work and knowing how to control them with the use of power and flight controls are essential to flight. [Figure 2-3] They are defined as follows:

summary.title: Aerodynamic Lift and Forces on a Helicopter Rotor Blade
summary.long_summary: The rotor blade described weighs 100 lb, spans 20 ft, and has a 1‑ft chord, giving a 20 sq ft surface area. When balanced on a pinpoint stand, the blade will fall unless an upward force equal to its weight is applied. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is 2,116 lb/ft², but it acts equally on both surfaces, producing no net force. A pressure differential of just 1 lb/ft² across the blade surface would generate an upward force of 100 lb, counteracting gravity. This differential is achieved by creating dynamic pressure over the airfoil: air moving faster over the upper surface lowers its static pressure, while slower flow beneath raises static pressure, producing lift. The aerodynamic force generated by moving air consists of lift (perpendicular to flow) and drag (parallel to flow). In helicopter flight, four aerodynamic forces act on the aircraft—thrust, drag, lift, and weight—and pilots control them via power and flight controls. By adjusting airflow over the rotor blades, sufficient lift can be produced to keep the blade suspended when the stand is removed, illustrating the fundamental principle behind helicopter lift.

topics.context:
• Lift—opposes the downward force of weight, is produced by the dynamic effect of the air acting on the airfoil and acts perpendicular to the flightpath through the center of lift.
  • Weight—the combined load of the aircraft itself, the crew, the fuel, and the cargo or baggage. Weight pulls the aircraft downward because of the force of gravity. It opposes lift and acts vertically downward through the aircraft's center of gravity (CG).
  • Thrust—the force produced by the power plant/propeller or rotor. It opposes or overcomes the force of drag. As a general rule, it acts parallel to the longitudinal axis. However, this is not always the case, as explained later.
  • Drag—a rearward, retarding force caused by disruption of airflow by the wing, rotor, fuselage, and other protruding objects. Drag opposes thrust and acts rearward parallel to the relative wind.

For a more in-depth explanation of general aerodynamics, refer to the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge.

Lift

Lift is generated when an object changes the direction of flow of a fluid or when the fluid is forced to move by the object passing through it. When the object and fluid move relative to each other and the object turns the fluid flow in a direction perpendicular to that flow, the force required to do this work creates an equal and opposite force that is lift. The object may be moving through a stationary fluid, or the fluid may be flowing past a stationary object—these two are effectively identical as, in principle, it is only the frame of reference of the viewer which differs. The lift generated by an airfoil depends on such factors as:

  • Speed of the airflow
  • Density of the air
  • Total area of the segment or airfoil
  • Angle of attack (AOA) between the air and the airfoil

The AOA is the angle at which the airfoil meets the oncoming airflow (or vice versa). In the case of a helicopter, the object is the rotor blade (airfoil) and the fluid is the air. Lift is produced when a mass of air is deflected, and it always acts perpendicular to the resultant relative wind. A symmetric airfoil must have a positive AOA to generate positive lift. At a zero AOA, no lift is generated. A cambered or nonsymmetrical airfoil may produce positive lift at zero, or even small negative AOA.

The basic concept of lift is simple. However, the details of how the relative movement of air and airfoil interact to produce the turning action that generates lift are complex. In any case causing lift, an angled flat plate, revolving cylinder, airfoil, etc., the flow meeting the leading edge of the object is forced to split over and under the object. The sudden change in direction over the object causes an area of low pressure to form behind the leading edge on the upper surface of the object. In turn, due to this pressure gradient and the viscosity of the fluid, the flow over the object is accelerated down along the upper surface of the object. At the same time, the flow forced under the object is rapidly slowed or stagnated causing an area of high pressure. This also causes the flow to accelerate along the upper surface of the object. The two sections of the fluid each leave the trailing edge of the object with a downward component of momentum, producing lift. [Figure 2-4]

Bernoulli's Principle

Bernoulli's principle describes the relationship between internal fluid pressure and fluid velocity. It is a statement of the law of conservation of energy and helps explain why an airfoil develops an aerodynamic force. The concept of conservation of energy states energy cannot be created or destroyed and the amount of energy entering a system must also exit. Specifically, in this case the “energy” referred to is the dynamic pressure (the kinetic energy of the air—more velocity, more kinetic energy) and static air pressure (potential energy). These will change among themselves, but the total pressure energy remains constant inside the tube.

A simple tube with a constricted portion near the center of its length illustrates this principle. An example is running water through a garden hose. The mass of flow per unit area (cross-sectional area of tube) is the mass flow rate. In Figure 2-5, the flow into the tube is constant, neither accelerating nor decelerating; thus, the mass flow rate through the tube must be the same at stations 1, 2, and 3. If the cross-sectional area at any one of these stations—or any given point—in the tube is reduced, the fluid velocity must increase to maintain a constant mass flow rate to move the same amount of fluid through a smaller area. The continuity of mass flow causes the air to move faster through the venturi. In other words, fluid speeds up in direct proportion to the reduction in area.

faqs.question: What factors affect the amount of lift an airfoil produces?

faqs.question: How does Bernoulli's principle relate to lift?

faqs.question: What happens to air pressure on the upper and lower surfaces of an airfoil?

faqs.question: How does the continuity of mass flow in a tube explain changes in fluid velocity?

summary.title: Fundamentals of Aerodynamic Forces and Lift Generation
summary.long_summary:
The passage outlines the four primary aerodynamic forces acting on an aircraft: lift, weight, thrust, and drag. Lift opposes weight and is produced by the dynamic effect of air on an airfoil, acting perpendicular to the flight path through the center of lift. Weight is the combined mass of the aircraft, crew, fuel, and cargo, pulling the aircraft downward through the center of gravity. Thrust, generated by the power plant, propeller, or rotor, overcomes drag and generally acts along the longitudinal axis, though variations exist. Drag is a rearward force caused by airflow disruption around the wing, fuselage, and other protrusions, opposing thrust.

Lift generation is explained in detail. It arises when an object changes the direction of a fluid flow, creating an equal and opposite reaction force. Key factors influencing lift include airflow speed, air density, wing (airfoil) area, and angle of attack (AOA). A positive AOA is required for a symmetric airfoil to produce lift; cambered airfoils can generate lift at zero or slight negative AOA. The flow over the upper surface accelerates, creating low pressure, while the flow under the wing slows, creating high pressure; the resulting pressure differential produces lift.

Bernoulli's principle is introduced as the relationship between fluid velocity and pressure, illustrating how a constricted flow area (as in a venturi) increases velocity and reduces static pressure, conserving total energy. This principle helps explain the pressure differences that develop over an airfoil during lift production. Even so, under the right set of adverse circumstances, such as high-density altitude, turbulent air, high gross weight, and poor pilot technique, sufficient or excess power may not be available to maintain altitude and airspeed. Pilots must take all of these factors into consideration throughout the entire flight from the point of ascending to a hover to landing. Above 30° of bank, the apparent increase in gross weight soars. At 30° of bank, or pitch, the apparent increase is only 16 percent, but at 60°, it is twice the load on the wings and rotor disk. For example, if the weight of the helicopter is 1,600 pounds, the weight supported by the rotor disk in a 30° bank at a constant altitude would be 1,856 pounds (1,600 + 16 percent (or 256)). In a 60° bank, it would be 3,200 pounds; in an 80° bank, it would be almost six times as much, or 8,000 pounds. It is important to note that each rotor blade must support a percentage of the gross weight. In a two-bladed system, each blade of the 1,600-pound helicopter as stated above would have to lift 50 percent or 800 pounds. If this same helicopter had three rotor blades, each blade would have to lift only 33 percent, or 533 pounds. One additional cause of large load factors is rough or turbulent air. The severe vertical gusts produced by turbulence can cause a sudden increase in AOA, resulting in increased rotor blade loads that are resisted by the inertia of the helicopter.

Each type of helicopter has its own limitations that are based on the aircraft structure, size, and capabilities. Regardless of how much weight one can carry or the engine power that it may have, they are all susceptible to aerodynamic overloading. Unfortunately, if the pilot attempts to push the performance envelope the consequence can be fatal. Aerodynamic forces effect every movement in a helicopter, whether it is increasing the collective or a steep bank angle. Anticipating results from a particular maneuver or adjustment of a flight control is not good piloting technique. Instead pilots need to truly understand the capabilities of the helicopter under any and all circumstances and plan never to exceed the flight envelope for any situation.

Thrust

Thrust, like lift, is generated by the rotation of the main rotor disk. In a helicopter, thrust can be forward, rearward, sideward, or vertical. The resultant lift and thrust determines the direction of movement of the helicopter.

The solidity ratio is the ratio of the total rotor blade area, which is the combined area of all the main rotor blades, to the total rotor disk area. This ratio provides a means to measure the potential for a rotor disk to provide thrust and lift. The mathematical calculations needed to calculate the solidity ratio for each helicopter may not be of importance to most pilots but what should be are the capabilities of the rotor disk to produce and maintain lift. Many helicopter accidents are caused from the rotor disk being overloaded. Simply put, pilots attempt maneuvers that require more lift than the rotor disk can produce or more power than the helicopter's powerplant can provide. Trying to land with a nose high attitude along with any other unfavorable condition (i.e., high gross weight or wind gusts) is most likely to end in disaster.

The tail rotor also produces thrust. The amount of thrust is variable through the use of the antitorque pedals and is used to control the helicopter's yaw.

Drag

The force that resists the movement of a helicopter through the air and is produced when lift is developed is called drag. Drag must be overcome by the engine to turn the rotor. Drag always acts parallel to the relative wind. Total drag is composed of three types of drag: profile, induced, and parasite.

Profile Drag

Profile drag develops from the frictional resistance of the blades passing through the air. It does not change significantly with the airfoil's AOA but increases moderately when airspeed increases. Profile drag is composed of form drag and skin friction. Form drag results from the turbulent wake caused by the separation of airflow from the surface of a structure. The amount of drag is related to both the size and shape of the structure that protrudes into the relative wind. [Figure 2-9]

Figure 2-9. It is easy to visualize the creation of form drag by examining the airflow around a flat plate. Streamlining decreases form drag by reducing the airflow separation.

summary.title: Helicopter Aerodynamic Loads, Thrust, and Drag Considerations
summary.long_summary:
The text explains how apparent gross weight rises with bank angle, remaining modest up to 30° but increasing sharply beyond that. At 30° bank the load is about 16 % higher; at 60° it doubles, and at 80° it can be six times the original weight. This extra load must be supported by each rotor blade, so helicopters with more blades share the burden (e.g., a three‑blade rotor carries one‑third of the weight per blade versus one‑half for a two‑blade system). Turbulent air and vertical gusts can further raise the angle of attack, producing sudden load spikes that may exceed the rotor’s capacity.

Every helicopter has structural and performance limits based on size, design, and power. Exceeding these limits—by demanding more lift or power than the rotor disk or engine can provide—can lead to fatal aerodynamic overload. Pilots must understand these limits under all conditions and avoid pushing the envelope.

Thrust in a helicopter is produced by the main rotor and can be directed forward, rearward, sideways, or vertically; the tail rotor provides variable thrust for yaw control via the anti‑torque pedals. The solidity ratio (blade area ÷ rotor disk area) indicates the rotor’s potential to generate thrust and lift, though pilots need only know the practical capability, not the exact calculation.

Drag opposes motion and must be overcome by engine power. It consists of profile drag (friction and form drag from blade surfaces), induced drag, and parasite drag. Profile drag grows modestly with airspeed and is linked to blade shape and surface roughness; streamlining reduces form drag by minimizing airflow separation, as illustrated in Figure 2‑9.

Overall, safe helicopter operation requires careful management of bank‑induced load factors, awareness of rotor‑disk limits, and understanding of thrust and drag forces.

Newton's Third Law of Motion

Additional lift is provided by the rotor blade's lower surface as air striking the underside is deflected downward. According to Newton's Third Law of Motion, "for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction," the air that is deflected downward also produces an upward (lifting) reaction.

Since air is much like water, the explanation for this source of lift may be compared to the planing effect of skis on water. The lift that supports the water skis (and the skier) is the force caused by the impact pressure and the deflection of water from the lower surfaces of the skis.

Under most flying conditions, the impact pressure and the deflection of air from the lower surface of the rotor blade provides a comparatively small percentage of the total lift. The majority of lift is the result of decreased pressure above the blade, rather than the increased pressure below it.

Weight

Normally, weight is thought of as being a known, fixed value, such as the weight of the helicopter, fuel, and occupants. To lift the helicopter off the ground vertically, the rotor disk must generate enough lift to overcome or offset the total weight of the helicopter and its occupants. Newton's First Law states: "Every object in a state of uniform motion tends to remain in that state of motion unless an external force is applied to it." In this case, the object is the helicopter whether at a hover or on the ground and the external force applied to it is lift, which is accomplished by increasing the pitch angle of the main rotor blades. This action forces the helicopter into a state of motion, without it the helicopter would either remain on the ground or at a hover.

The weight of the helicopter can also be influenced by aerodynamic loads. When you bank a helicopter while maintaining a constant altitude, the "G" load or load factor increases. The load factor is the actual load on the rotor blades at any time, divided by the normal load or gross weight (weight of the helicopter and its contents). Any time a helicopter flies in a constant altitude curved flightpath, the load supported by the rotor blades is greater than the total weight of the helicopter. The tighter the curved flightpath is, the steeper the bank is; the more rapid the flare or pullout from a dive is, the greater the load supported by the rotor. Therefore, the greater the load factor must be. [Figure 2-8]

faqs.question: What is Venturi flow and how does it affect the pressure on a rotor blade?
faqs.answer: Venturi flow occurs when air moves through a tube that narrows in the middle, causing the flow to accelerate. In the rotor blade, the upper air layers restrict the flow over the curved area, accelerating the air and creating a decrease in static pressure above the blade, which contributes to lift.

faqs.question: Why do the upper air layers restrict the flow over the curved portion of the rotor blade?
faqs.answer: The upper air layers act like the top half of a constricted tube, limiting the space through which the air can move. This restriction forces the air to accelerate over the curved portion, lowering the static pressure there.

faqs.question: How does Newton’s Third Law of Motion provide additional lift on a helicopter rotor blade?
faqs.answer: According to Newton’s Third Law, the air that is struck on the underside of the rotor blade is deflected downward. The downward deflection of the air creates an equal and opposite upward reaction force, adding to the overall lift.

faqs.question: Is the lift generated by the lower surface of the rotor blade a major contributor to total lift?
faqs.answer: No. Under most flying conditions, the lift from impact pressure and deflection of air on the lower surface is a comparatively small percentage of the total lift. The majority of lift comes from the decreased pressure above the blade.

faqs.question: What does “weight” refer to in the context of helicopter flight?
faqs.answer: Weight refers to the total mass that must be lifted, including the helicopter’s structure, fuel, occupants, and any other payload. The rotor disk must generate enough lift to overcome or offset this total weight to achieve vertical lift.

faqs.question: How does banking a helicopter affect the load factor and required lift?
faqs.answer: When a helicopter banks while maintaining constant altitude, the load factor (the actual load on the rotor blades divided by the gross weight) increases. A higher load factor means the rotor blades must produce more lift to support the increased aerodynamic load.

faqs.question: What happens if the helicopter does not have enough engine power to meet the increased load factor during a banked turn?
faqs.answer: If excess engine power is not available, the helicopter will either descend or must decelerate in order to maintain the same altitude, because it cannot produce the additional lift required by the higher load factor.

faqs.question: How can a pilot determine the amount of “G” loading for a given bank angle?
faqs.answer: A pilot can use the load factor diagram (Figure 2‑8), which plots load factor in Gs against bank angle in degrees. The diagram shows that load factor rises rapidly as bank angle increases, reaching about 9 Gs at an 80‑degree bank.

faqs.question: Why is the lift from the rotor’s lower surface compared to the planing effect of skis on water?
faqs.answer: Both involve an impact pressure and deflection of a fluid (air for the rotor, water for skis). The lift generated by the rotor’s lower surface is analogous to the upward force that supports a skier on water skis, caused by the water being deflected downward.

summary.title: Helicopter Lift Mechanisms and Load‑Factor Effects
summary.long_summary:
The passage explains how a helicopter’s rotor generates lift. Figure 2‑7 illustrates Venturi flow: as air passes through the narrowed middle of a tube, it accelerates, lowering static pressure above the curved surface and creating a pressure differential. Newton’s Third Law adds that air striking the rotor’s lower surface is deflected downward, producing an upward reaction, similar to the planing effect of skis on water. However, this lower‑surface contribution is minor; most lift comes from the reduced pressure on the upper side of the blade. 

Weight, defined as the helicopter’s mass plus fuel and occupants, must be overcome by lift. According to Newton’s First Law, lift (generated by increasing rotor blade pitch) is the external force that moves the helicopter from rest or hover. When a helicopter banks while maintaining altitude, the load factor (G‑load) rises: the rotor must support more than the helicopter’s static weight. Figure 2‑8 shows the relationship between bank angle and load factor, reaching about 9 G at an 80° bank. Higher load factors require additional lift; if engine power is insufficient, the aircraft must descend or decelerate to keep altitude. Thus, lift production, pressure differentials, and load‑factor management are critical for safe helicopter flight.

### Airflow in Forward Flight

Airflow across the rotor disk in forward flight varies from airflow at a hover. In forward flight, air flows opposite the aircraft's flightpath. faqs.question: Which part of the rotor disk experiences the lowest airflow velocity in forward flight?

faqs.question: What happens to the advancing blade as its relative wind speed increases?

faqs.question: What happens to the retreating blade as its relative wind speed decreases?
faqs.answer: The retreating blade loses lift and begins to flap downward. Its maximum down‑flap occurs at the 9 o’clock position, where the relative wind speed is the lowest.

faqs.question: How does the up‑flap of the advancing blade affect the airflow and angle of attack?

faqs.question: How do changes in power or cyclic input affect the helicopter’s altitude before level flight is established?
faqs.answer: Any change in power or cyclic input causes the helicopter to either climb or descend until straight‑and‑level flight is re‑established.

summary.title: Helicopter Forward‑Flight Aerodynamics and Blade Airflow Dynamics
summary.long_summary: In forward flight the airflow across a helicopter’s rotor disk differs from hover because the aircraft’s forward speed adds a wind component opposite the flight path. The relative wind speed a blade experiences depends on its azimuth position: the advancing blade (right side, 3 o’clock) meets the sum of its rotational speed and forward‑air speed, giving the highest airflow velocity and lift, while the retreating blade (left side, 9 o’clock) meets the difference, resulting in the lowest velocity and reduced lift. Blades over the nose and tail (positions B and D) encounter airflow essentially equal to their rotational speed alone. As the advancing blade’s relative wind increases, it generates more lift and flaps upward, producing a downward induced flow that effectively reduces its angle of attack. Conversely, the retreating blade loses lift as its relative wind drops, flaps downward, and its angle of attack increases. These cyclic variations create a changing lift distribution across the rotor disk, influencing the helicopter’s pitch, roll, and power requirements. Once straight‑and‑level flight is achieved, pilots record the torque (power) setting and avoid major control adjustments, as illustrated in the power‑versus‑airspeed chart (Figure 2‑34).

Skin friction is caused by surface roughness. Even though the surface appears smooth, it may be quite rough when viewed under a microscope. A thin layer of air clings to the rough surface and creates small eddies that contribute to drag.

Induced Drag

Induced drag is generated by the airflow circulation around the rotor blade as it creates lift. The high-pressure area beneath the blade joins the low-pressure area above the blade at the trailing edge and at the rotor tips. This causes a spiral, or vortex, which trails behind each blade whenever lift is being produced. These vortices deflect the airstream downward in the vicinity of the blade, creating an increase in downwash. Therefore, the blade operates in an average relative wind that is inclined downward and rearward near the blade. Because the lift produced by the blade is perpendicular to the relative wind, the lift is inclined aft by the same amount. The component of lift that is acting in a rearward direction is induced drag. [Figure 2-10]

As the air pressure differential increases with an increase in AOA, stronger vortices form, and induced drag increases. Since the blade's AOA is usually lower at higher airspeeds, and higher at low speeds, induced drag decreases as airspeed increases and increases as airspeed decreases. Induced drag is the major cause of drag at lower airspeeds.

Parasite Drag

Parasite drag is present any time the helicopter is moving through the air. This type of drag increases with airspeed. Non-lifting components of the helicopter, such as the cabin, rotor mast, tail, and landing gear, contribute to parasite drag. Any loss of momentum by the airstream, due to such things as openings for engine cooling, creates additional parasite drag. Because of its rapid increase with increasing airspeed, parasite drag is the major cause of drag at higher airspeeds. Parasite drag varies with the square of the velocity; therefore, doubling the airspeed increases the parasite drag four times.

Total Drag

Total drag for a helicopter is the sum of all three drag forces. [Figure 2-11] As airspeed increases, parasite drag increases, while induced drag decreases. Profile drag remains relatively constant throughout the speed range with some increase at higher airspeeds. Combining all drag forces results in a total drag curve. The low point on the total drag curve shows the airspeed at which drag is minimized. This is the point where the lift-to-drag ratio is greatest and is referred to as L/D_{MAX}. At this speed, the total lift capacity of the helicopter, when compared to the total drag of the helicopter, is most favorable. This is an important factor in helicopter performance.

Airfoil

Helicopters are able to fly due to aerodynamic forces produced when air passes around the airfoil. An airfoil is any surface producing more lift than drag when passing through the air at a suitable angle. Airfoils are most often associated with production of lift. Airfoils are also used for stability (fin), control (elevator), and thrust or propulsion (propeller or rotor). Certain airfoils, such as rotor blades, combine some of these functions. The main and tail rotor blades of the helicopter are airfoils, and air is forced to pass around the blades by mechanically powered rotation. In some conditions, parts of the fuselage, such as the vertical and horizontal stabilizers, can become airfoils. Airfoils are carefully structured to accommodate a specific set of flight characteristics.

faqs.question: What causes skin friction drag on a helicopter surface?
faqs.answer: Skin friction is caused by surface roughness; even a surface that looks smooth can be rough at a microscopic level, allowing a thin layer of air to cling to it and create small eddies that contribute to drag.

faqs.question: How is induced drag generated on a rotor blade?
faqs.answer: Induced drag is generated by the circulation of airflow around the rotor blade that creates lift; the high‑pressure area beneath the blade joins the low‑pressure area above it at the trailing edge and rotor tips, forming a vortex that deflects the airstream downward, causing the lift vector to be inclined rearward and creating a rearward component of lift known as induced drag.

faqs.question: Why does induced drag increase when the angle of attack (AOA) increases?
faqs.answer: As the air‑pressure differential grows with a higher AOA, stronger vortices form, which increase the downwash and therefore increase induced drag.

faqs.question: How does airspeed affect induced drag?
faqs.answer: Induced drag decreases as airspeed increases because the blade’s AOA is usually lower at higher airspeeds, and it increases as airspeed decreases.

faqs.question: What components of a helicopter contribute to parasite drag?
faqs.answer: Parasite drag is produced by non‑lifting components such as the cabin, rotor mast, tail, landing gear, and any openings for engine cooling that cause loss of momentum in the airstream.

faqs.question: How does parasite drag change with airspeed?
faqs.answer: Parasite drag varies with the square of the velocity; doubling the airspeed increases parasite drag fourfold.

faqs.question: What is the relationship between total drag, parasite drag, and induced drag as airspeed changes?
faqs.answer: As airspeed increases, parasite drag increases while induced drag decreases; the total drag curve is the sum of these forces (plus relatively constant profile drag), showing a minimum point where drag is minimized.

faqs.question: What does the minimum point on the total drag curve represent?
faqs.answer: The low point on the total drag curve indicates the airspeed at which drag is minimized, the lift‑to‑drag ratio (L/D) is greatest (L/Dₘₐₓ), and the helicopter’s total lift capacity relative to its total drag is most favorable.

faqs.question: How is an airfoil defined in the context of helicopters?
faqs.answer: An airfoil is any surface that produces more lift than drag when moving through the air at a suitable angle; rotor blades, stabilizers, and sometimes parts of the fuselage act as airfoils to generate lift, provide stability, control, or thrust.

summary.title: Helicopter Drag Forces and Airfoil Fundamentals
summary.long_summary: The passage explains the aerodynamic forces affecting helicopters. Skin friction arises from microscopic surface roughness that traps a thin air layer, creating small eddies and drag. Induced drag is produced when lift-generating rotor blades cause high‑pressure air beneath the blade to meet low‑pressure air above at the trailing edge and tips, forming vortices that deflect the airstream downward. This downwash tilts the relative wind rearward, so a component of lift acts rearward as induced drag. Induced drag grows with angle of attack and is dominant at low airspeeds, decreasing as speed rises. Parasite drag exists whenever the helicopter moves through air; it increases with the square of velocity and is caused by non‑lifting parts such as the cabin, mast, tail, landing gear, and cooling openings. At high speeds parasite drag becomes the primary drag source. Total drag is the sum of induced, parasite, and profile drag; as speed increases, parasite drag rises while induced drag falls, producing a drag curve whose minimum point corresponds to the maximum lift‑to‑drag ratio (L/Dₘₐₓ). The text also defines an airfoil as any surface that generates more lift than drag at a suitable angle, noting that rotor blades, stabilizers, and propellers function as airfoils designed for specific flight characteristics. Key terminology such as blade span is introduced.

• Chord line—a straight line intersecting leading and trailing edges of the airfoil. [Figure 2-12]
  • Chord—the length of the chord line from leading edge to trailing edge; it is the characteristic longitudinal dimension of the airfoil section.
  • Mean camber line—a line drawn halfway between the upper and lower surfaces of the airfoil. [Figure 2-12]

The chord line connects the ends of the mean camber line. Camber refers to curvature of the airfoil and may be considered as curvature of the mean camber line. The shape of the mean camber is important for determining aerodynamic characteristics of an airfoil section. Maximum camber (displacement of the mean camber line from the chord line) and its location help to define the shape of the mean camber line. The location of maximum camber and its displacement from the chord line are expressed as fractions or percentages of the basic chord length. By varying the point of maximum camber, the manufacturer can tailor an airfoil for a specific purpose. The profile thickness and thickness distribution are important properties of an airfoil section.

  • Leading edge—the front edge of an airfoil. [Figure 2-12]
  • Flightpath velocity—the speed and direction of the airfoil passing through the air. For airfoils on an airplane, the flightpath velocity is equal to true airspeed (TAS). For helicopter rotor blades, flightpath velocity is equal to rotational velocity, plus or minus a component of directional airspeed. The rotational velocity of the rotor blade is lowest closer to the hub and increases outward towards the tip of the blade during rotation.
  • Relative wind—defined as the airflow relative to an airfoil and is created by movement of an airfoil through the air. This is rotational relative wind for rotary-wing aircraft and is covered in detail later. As an induced airflow may modify flightpath velocity, relative wind experienced by the airfoil may not be exactly opposite its direction of travel.
  • Trailing edge—the rearmost edge of an airfoil.
  • Induced flow—the downward flow of air through the rotor disk.
  • Resultant relative wind—relative wind modified by induced flow.
  • AOA—the angle measured between the resultant relative wind and chord line.
  • Angle of incidence (AOI)—the angle between the chord line of a blade and rotor hub. It is usually referred to as blade pitch angle. For fixed airfoils, such as vertical fins or elevators, angle of incidence is the angle between the chord line of the airfoil and a selected reference plane of the helicopter.
  • Center of pressure—the point along the chord line of an airfoil through which all aerodynamic forces are considered to act. Since pressures vary on the surface of an airfoil, an average location of pressure variation is needed. As the AOA changes, these pressures change, and the center of pressure moves along the chord line.

Airfoil Types

Symmetrical Airfoil

The symmetrical airfoil is distinguished by having identical upper and lower surfaces. [Figure 2-13] The mean camber line and chord line are the same on a symmetrical airfoil, and it produces no lift at zero AOA. Most light helicopters incorporate symmetrical airfoils in the main rotor blades.

Nonsymmetrical Airfoil (Cambered)

The nonsymmetrical airfoil has different upper and lower surfaces, with a greater curvature of the airfoil above the chord line than below. faqs.question: What is the chord line of an airfoil?
faqs.answer: The chord line is a straight line that connects the leading edge and the trailing edge of the airfoil.

faqs.question: How is the chord of an airfoil defined?
faqs.answer: The chord is the length of the chord line measured from the leading edge to the trailing edge and is the characteristic longitudinal dimension of the airfoil section.

faqs.question: What is the mean camber line and why is it important?
faqs.answer: The mean camber line is a line drawn halfway between the upper and lower surfaces of the airfoil. Its shape is important for determining the aerodynamic characteristics of the airfoil section.

faqs.question: What does “maximum camber” refer to and how is it expressed?
faqs.answer: Maximum camber is the greatest displacement of the mean camber line from the chord line. Its location and displacement are expressed as fractions or percentages of the basic chord length.

faqs.question: How do flightpath velocity and relative wind differ for an airfoil?
faqs.answer: Flightpath velocity is the speed and direction of the airfoil moving through the air (equal to true airspeed for airplanes or rotational velocity for rotor blades). Relative wind is the airflow relative to the airfoil created by its movement, which may be modified by induced flow and therefore not exactly opposite the flightpath velocity.

faqs.question: How is angle of attack (AOA) defined?
faqs.answer: AOA is the angle measured between the resultant relative wind (relative wind modified by induced flow) and the chord line of the airfoil.

faqs.question: What is the angle of incidence (AOI) and how is it used for rotor blades versus fixed airfoils?
faqs.answer: AOI is the angle between the chord line of a blade and the rotor hub, commonly called the blade pitch angle. For fixed airfoils such as vertical fins or elevators, AOI is the angle between the chord line and a selected reference plane of the helicopter.

faqs.question: What is the center of pressure on an airfoil?
faqs.answer: The center of pressure is the point along the chord line where all aerodynamic forces are considered to act; it moves along the chord line as the angle of attack changes.

faqs.question: What distinguishes a symmetrical airfoil from a nonsymmetrical (cambered) airfoil?
faqs.answer: A symmetrical airfoil has identical upper and lower surfaces, making the mean camber line and chord line the same and producing no lift at zero AOA. A nonsymmetrical (cambered) airfoil has different upper and lower surfaces with greater curvature above the chord line, resulting in a different mean camber line and the ability to generate lift at zero AOA.

faqs.question: Why are symmetrical airfoils commonly used in the main rotor blades of light helicopters?
faqs.answer: Symmetrical airfoils are used because their identical upper and lower surfaces provide consistent aerodynamic behavior and are well suited for the varying angles of attack experienced by rotor blades.

summary.title: Airfoil Geometry and Types Overview
summary.long_summary: The passage defines essential airfoil terminology. The chord line is a straight line joining the leading and trailing edges, while the chord is its length, representing the longitudinal dimension of the section. The mean camber line runs midway between the upper and lower surfaces; its curvature (camber) influences aerodynamic performance. Maximum camber and its position are expressed as fractions of the chord, allowing designers to tailor lift characteristics. Additional terms include the leading edge (front), trailing edge (rear), flight‑path velocity (airfoil speed through the air, equal to true airspeed for fixed‑wing aircraft or rotational speed for rotor blades), relative wind (airflow relative to the moving airfoil), induced flow (downwash through a rotor disk), and resultant relative wind (relative wind altered by induced flow). The angle of attack (AOA) is measured between the resultant wind and the chord line, whereas the angle of incidence (AOI) is the angle between the chord line and the rotor hub or a reference plane. The center of pressure is the point along the chord where aerodynamic forces can be considered to act, shifting with AOA changes. Two airfoil families are described: symmetrical airfoils have identical upper and lower surfaces, zero lift at zero AOA, and are common in light‑helicopter rotors; nonsymmetrical (cambered) airfoils have differing curvatures, generate lift at zero AOA, and are used where lift is needed without pitch. Figures illustrate these concepts.

Resultant Relative Wind

The resultant relative wind at a hover is rotational relative wind modified by induced flow. This is inclined downward at some angle and opposite the effective flightpath of the airfoil, rather than the physical flightpath (rotational relative wind). The resultant relative wind also serves as the reference plane for development of lift, drag, and total aerodynamic force (TAF) vectors on the airfoil. [Figure 2-20] When the helicopter has horizontal motion, airspeed further modifies the resultant relative wind. The airspeed component of relative wind results from the helicopter moving through the air. This airspeed component is added to, or subtracted from, the rotational relative wind depending on whether the blade is advancing or retreating in relation to helicopter movement. Introduction of airspeed relative wind also modifies induced flow. Generally, the downward velocity of induced flow is reduced. The pattern of air circulation through the disk changes when the aircraft has horizontal motion. As the helicopter gains airspeed, the addition of

forward velocity results in decreased induced flow velocity. This change results in an improved efficiency (additional lift) being produced from a given blade pitch setting.

Induced Flow (Downwash)

At flat pitch, air leaves the trailing edge of the rotor blade in the same direction it moved across the leading edge; no lift or induced flow is being produced. As blade pitch angle is increased, the rotor disk induces a downward flow of air through the rotor blades creating a downward component of air that is added to the rotational relative wind. Because the blades are moving horizontally, some of the air is displaced downward. The blades travel along the same path and pass a given point in rapid succession. Rotor blade action changes the still air to a column of descending air. Therefore, each blade has a decreased AOA due to the downwash. This downward flow of air is called induced flow (downwash). It is most pronounced at a hover under no-wind conditions. [Figure 2-21]

Figure 2-21. A helicopter in forward flight, or hovering with a headwind or crosswind, has more molecules of air entering the aft portion of the rotor disk. Therefore, at the rear of the rotor disk, the angle of attack is less and the induced flow is greater.

faqs.question: What is resultant relative wind and how does it differ from rotational relative wind?

faqs.question: How does induced flow affect the resultant relative wind at hover?
faqs.answer: Induced flow adds a downward component to the rotational relative wind, creating the downward‑inclined resultant relative wind that serves as the reference plane for lift, drag, and total aerodynamic force vectors.

faqs.question: How does horizontal motion (airspeed) modify the resultant relative wind?
faqs.answer: When the helicopter moves horizontally, an airspeed component of relative wind is added to or subtracted from the rotational relative wind depending on whether a blade is advancing or retreating, and this also modifies the induced flow.

faqs.question: Why does forward airspeed reduce the induced flow velocity?
faqs.answer: The forward‑velocity component of the relative wind reduces the downward velocity of induced flow, decreasing the overall induced flow velocity as the helicopter gains airspeed.

faqs.question: How does reduced induced flow improve helicopter efficiency?
faqs.answer: A lower induced‑flow velocity means the rotor produces additional lift for the same blade‑pitch setting, resulting in improved aerodynamic efficiency.

faqs.question: What is induced flow (downwash) and when is it most pronounced?
faqs.answer: Induced flow, also called downwash, is the downward flow of air created by the rotor disk when blade pitch is increased; it is most pronounced during a hover under no‑wind conditions.

faqs.question: How does blade pitch influence induced flow and lift generation?
faqs.answer: At flat pitch no lift or induced flow is produced; as blade pitch angle increases, the rotor disk induces a downward flow of air (induced flow) which, together with the blade’s motion, generates lift.

faqs.question: How does induced flow affect the angle of attack of rotor blades?
faqs.answer: The downward flow of induced air reduces the effective angle of attack of each blade because the blade encounters the air at a lower relative angle.

faqs.question: In forward flight or with a headwind/crosswind, how does airflow differ between the fore and aft portions of the rotor disk?
faqs.answer: More air molecules enter the aft portion of the rotor disk, resulting in a lower angle of attack and greater induced flow at the rear, while the fore portion experiences less induced flow and a higher angle of attack.

faqs.question: What role does the resultant relative wind play in determining lift, drag, and total aerodynamic force vectors?
faqs.answer: The resultant relative wind serves as the reference plane from which lift, drag, and total aerodynamic force (TAF) vectors on the airfoil are developed.

summary.title: Resultant Relative Wind and Induced Flow in Helicopter Rotors
summary.long_summary:
The text explains the aerodynamic environment of a helicopter rotor. At hover, the rotor experiences a rotational relative wind that is modified by induced flow—a downward‑moving column of air created when blade pitch generates lift. This combination forms the resultant relative wind, which is inclined downward and serves as the reference for lift, drag, and total aerodynamic force vectors on the airfoil. When the helicopter moves horizontally, an additional airspeed component adds to or subtracts from the rotational wind depending on whether a blade is advancing or retreating. This airspeed also reduces the magnitude of induced flow, decreasing downwash velocity and improving lift efficiency for a given blade pitch. 

Induced flow (downwash) is absent at flat pitch because the blade does not generate lift. As pitch increases, the rotor induces a downward airflow that combines with the rotational wind, lowering the effective angle of attack on each blade. The effect is strongest in hover with no wind. In forward flight, or when encountering headwinds or crosswinds, more air enters the aft portion of the rotor disk, resulting in greater induced flow and a reduced angle of attack there, while the fore portion experiences less induced flow and a higher angle of attack. This variation influences lift distribution and overall rotor performance.

topics.title: Page 12
topics.context:
In Ground Effect (IGE)

Ground effect is the increased efficiency of the rotor disk caused by interference of the airflow when near the ground. The air pressure or density is increased, which acts to decrease the downward velocity of air. Ground effect permits relative wind to be more horizontal, lift vector to be more vertical, and induced drag to be reduced. These conditions allow the rotor disk to be more efficient. Maximum ground effect is achieved when hovering over smooth hard surfaces. When hovering over surfaces as tall grass, trees, bushes, rough terrain, and water, maximum ground effect is reduced. Rotor efficiency is increased by ground effect to a height of about one rotor diameter (measured from the ground to the rotor disk) for most helicopters. Since the induced flow velocities are decreased, the AOA is increased, which requires a reduced blade pitch angle and a reduction in induced drag. This reduces the power required to hover IGE. [Figure 2-22]

Out of Ground Effect (OGE)

The benefit of placing the helicopter near the ground is lost above IGE altitude. Above this altitude, the power required to hover remains nearly constant, given similar conditions (such as wind). Induced flow velocity is increased, resulting in a decrease in AOA and a decrease in lift. Under the correct circumstances, this downward flow can become so localized that the helicopter and locally disturbed air will sink at alarming rates. This effect is called vortex ring state (formerly referenced as settling-with-power) and is discussed at length in Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards. A higher blade pitch angle is required to maintain the same AOA as in IGE hover. The increased pitch angle also creates more drag. This increased pitch angle and drag requires more power to hover OGE than IGE. [Figure 2-23]

Rotor Blade Angles

There are two angles that enable a rotor disk to produce the lift required for a helicopter to fly: angle of incidence and angle of attack.

Angle of Incidence

Angle of incidence is the angle between the chord line of a main or tail rotor blade and its rotor disk. It is a mechanical angle rather than an aerodynamic angle and is sometimes referred to as blade pitch angle. [Figure 2-24] In the absence of induced flow, AOA and angle of incidence are the same. Whenever induced flow, up flow (inflow), or airspeed modifies the relative wind, the AOA is different from the angle of incidence. Collective input and cyclic feathering (see page 2-12) change the angle of incidence. A change in the angle of incidence changes the AOA, which changes the coefficient of lift, thereby changing the lift produced by the airfoil.

faqs.question: What is ground effect (IGE) and how does it affect a helicopter’s rotor efficiency?

The airflow is interfered with, raising air pressure or density and decreasing the downward velocity of the air. This makes the relative wind more horizontal, the lift vector more vertical, and reduces induced drag, allowing the rotor to be more efficient.

faqs.question: How does the type of surface under the helicopter influence ground effect?
faqs.answer: Maximum ground effect is achieved when hovering over smooth, hard surfaces. Hovering over tall grass, trees, bushes, rough terrain, or water reduces the amount of ground effect that can be obtained.

faqs.question: Up to what height does ground effect improve rotor efficiency?
faqs.answer: Rotor efficiency is increased by ground effect to a height of about one rotor diameter measured from the ground to the rotor disk for most helicopters.

faqs.question: What happens to the power required to hover when the helicopter moves out of ground effect (OGE)?
faqs.answer: Above the IGE altitude the benefit of ground effect is lost, and the power required to hover remains nearly constant (given similar conditions). More power is needed OGE because a higher blade pitch angle is required to maintain the same angle of attack, which also creates more drag.

faqs.question: Why is a higher blade pitch angle needed when hovering OGE?
faqs.answer: When the helicopter is OGE, induced flow velocity increases, which decreases the angle of attack and lift. To keep the same angle of attack as in IGE hover, the blade pitch angle must be increased, resulting in more drag and higher power demand.

faqs.question: What is vortex ring state and when can it occur?
faqs.answer: Vortex ring state is a condition where the downward flow becomes highly localized, causing the helicopter and the disturbed air around it to sink rapidly. It can occur when the helicopter is OGE and the induced flow is insufficient to maintain lift.

faqs.question: What is the angle of incidence of a rotor blade?
faqs.answer: Angle of incidence is the mechanical angle between the chord line of a main or tail rotor blade and the rotor disk. It is also referred to as the blade pitch angle.

faqs.question: How does angle of incidence differ from angle of attack?
faqs.answer: Angle of incidence is a fixed mechanical angle, while angle of attack is the aerodynamic angle between the relative wind and the blade’s chord line. In the absence of induced flow they are the same, but induced flow, upflow, or airspeed change the relative wind, making the angle of attack different from the angle of incidence.

faqs.question: How do collective input and cyclic feathering affect the rotor blade angles?
faqs.answer: Collective input and cyclic feathering change the angle of incidence. A change in the angle of incidence alters the angle of attack, which changes the coefficient of lift and therefore the lift produced by the airfoil.

summary.title: Helicopter Ground Effect and Rotor Blade Angles
summary.long_summary:
Ground effect (IGE) occurs when a helicopter hovers close to the ground, typically within one rotor diameter. The proximity interferes with the downwash, increasing air pressure and density, which reduces the downward velocity of the airflow. This makes the relative wind more horizontal, the lift vector more vertical, and induced drag lower, allowing the rotor disk to operate more efficiently and requiring less power to hover. Maximum IGE is achieved over smooth, hard surfaces; rough terrain, vegetation, or water diminish the effect.

When the helicopter rises above the IGE altitude (OGE), the benefits disappear. Induced flow velocity rises, decreasing angle of attack and lift, so a higher blade pitch angle is needed to maintain lift. The increased pitch creates more drag, demanding more power to hover. In extreme cases, localized downwash can cause vortex ring state, a dangerous rapid sink.

Rotor lift is governed by two angles: angle of incidence (mechanical blade pitch relative to the rotor disk) and angle of attack (aerodynamic angle between chord line and relative wind). Collective and cyclic controls alter the angle of incidence, which in turn changes the angle of attack, lift coefficient, and ultimately the lift produced. Without induced flow, the two angles are identical; induced flow separates them.
summary.short_summary: Ground effect improves hover efficiency; OGE requires more power

Cyclic feathering changes the blade's AOA differentially around the rotor disk and creates a differential lift. Aviators use cyclic feathering to control attitude of the rotor disk. It is the means to control rearward tilt of the rotor (blowback) caused by flapping action and (along with blade flapping) counteract dissymmetry of lift (discussed in chapter 3). Cyclic feathering causes attitude of the rotor disk to change but does not change the amount of net lift the rotor disk is producing. Most of the changes in AOA come from change in airspeed and rate of climb or descent; others such as flapping occur automatically due to the rotor system design. Flapping is the up and down movement of rotor blades about a hinge on a fully articulated rotor system. A semi-rigid system does not have a hinge but flap as a unit. A rigid rotor system has no vertical or horizontal hinges, so the blades cannot flap or drag, but they can flex. By flexing, the blades themselves compensate for the forces which previously required rugged hinges. It occurs in response to changes in lift due to changing velocity or cyclic feathering. No flapping occurs when the tip-path plane is perpendicular to the mast. The flapping action alone, or along with cyclic feathering, controls dissymmetry of lift. Flapping is the primary means of compensating for dissymmetry of lift. Pilots adjust AOA through normal control manipulation of the pitch angle of the blades. If the pitch angle is increased, the AOA increases; if the pitch angle is reduced, the AOA is reduced. ### Powered Flight In powered flight (hovering, vertical, forward, sideward, or rearward), the total lift and thrust forces of a rotor are perpendicular to the rotor disk. ### Hovering Flight Hovering is the most challenging part of flying a helicopter. This is because a helicopter generates its own gusty air while in a hover, which acts against the fuselage and flight control surfaces. The end result is constant control inputs and corrections by the pilot to keep the helicopter where it is required to be. Despite the complexity of the task, the control inputs in a hover are simple. The cyclic is used to eliminate drift in the horizontal plane, controlling forward, backward, right and left movement or travel. The throttle, if not governor controlled, is used to control revolutions per minute (rpm). The collective is used to maintain altitude. The pedals are used to control nose direction or heading. It is the interaction of these controls that makes hovering difficult, since an adjustment in any one control requires an adjustment of the other two, creating a cycle of constant correction. During hovering flight, a helicopter maintains a constant position over a selected point, usually a few feet above the ground. The ability of the helicopter to hover comes from the both the lift component, which is the force developed by the main rotor(s) to overcome gravity and aircraft weight, and the thrust component, which acts horizontally to accelerate or decelerate the helicopter in the desired direction. Pilots direct the thrust of the rotor disk by using the cyclic to rotate the rotor disk plane relative to the horizon. They do this in order to induce travel or compensate for the wind and hold a position. At a hover in a no-wind condition, all opposing forces (lift, thrust, drag, and weight) are in balance; they are equal and opposite. Therefore, lift and weight are equal, resulting in the helicopter remaining at a stationary hover. [Figure 2-26] While hovering, the amount of main rotor thrust can be adjusted to maintain the desired hovering height. This is done by changing the angle of incidence (by moving the collective) of the rotor blades, and hence their AOA. Changing the AOA changes the drag on the rotor blades, and the power delivered by the engine must change as well to keep the rotor speed constant. The weight that must be supported is the total weight of the helicopter and its occupants. If the amount of lift is greater than the actual weight, the helicopter accelerates upwards until the lift force equals the weight of the helicopter; if lift is less than weight, the helicopter accelerates downward. The drag of a hovering helicopter is mainly induced drag incurred while the blades are producing lift. There is, however, some profile drag on the blades as they rotate through the air and a small amount of parasite drag from the non-lift-producing surfaces of the helicopter, such as the rotor hub, cowlings, and

faqs.question: What does cyclic feathering do to the rotor disk?

faqs.question: How does cyclic feathering help counter dissymmetry of lift?
faqs.answer: By varying the AOA around the rotor disk, cyclic feathering creates differential lift that, together with blade flapping, counteracts the dissymmetry of lift that occurs when the rotor advances into the relative wind.

faqs.question: What is the primary means of compensating for dissymmetry of lift?
faqs.answer: Flapping is the primary means of compensating for dissymmetry of lift; it allows the blades to move up and down to equalize lift across the rotor disk.

faqs.question: How do different rotor systems handle flapping?
faqs.answer: A fully articulated rotor system has hinges that allow each blade to flap individually. A semi‑rigid system has no individual hinges but the blades flap together as a unit. A rigid rotor system has no vertical or horizontal hinges; the blades flex to compensate for lift changes instead of flapping.

faqs.question: How do pilots change the angle of attack of the rotor blades?
faqs.answer: Pilots change the blade pitch angle: increasing the pitch angle increases the AOA, while reducing the pitch angle decreases the AOA.

faqs.question: What forces act on a helicopter during a hover in no‑wind conditions?
faqs.answer: In a no‑wind hover, lift balances weight (vertical forces) and thrust balances drag (horizontal forces), so the four forces are equal and opposite, keeping the helicopter stationary.

faqs.question: Which controls are used to maintain altitude, position, and heading while hovering?
faqs.answer: The collective controls altitude by changing blade AOA, the cyclic eliminates horizontal drift and directs thrust, the throttle (if not governor‑controlled) sets rotor RPM, and the pedals control nose direction (heading).

faqs.question: Why is hovering considered the most challenging phase of helicopter flight?
faqs.answer: Hovering is challenging because the helicopter creates its own gusty air that constantly pushes against the fuselage and controls, requiring continuous pilot inputs and constant correction of all three primary controls (cyclic, collective, throttle/pedals).

faqs.question: How is thrust directed during hover to move the helicopter or counter wind?
faqs.answer: Pilots rotate the rotor‑disk plane relative to the horizon with the cyclic, which tilts the thrust vector in the desired direction, allowing travel or compensation for wind while hovering.

faqs.question: What types of drag affect a hovering helicopter?
faqs.answer: The drag on a hovering helicopter consists mainly of induced drag from the lifting blades, profile drag on the rotating blades, and a small amount of parasite drag from non‑lifting components such as the rotor hub and cowlings.

summary.title: Cyclic Feathering, Flapping, and Hover Control in Helicopters
summary.long_summary:
Cyclic feathering varies the blade angle of attack (AOA) around the rotor disk, producing differential lift that tilts the rotor disk but does not alter the total lift generated. This control method is used by pilots to manage the rearward tilt (blow‑back) caused by blade flapping and to counteract dissymmetry of lift. Blade flapping—up‑and‑down movement about a hinge in fully articulated rotors, collective motion in semi‑rigid systems, or flexing in rigid rotors—also compensates for lift differences across the disk. Together, cyclic feathering and flapping adjust rotor disk attitude and are the primary means of handling dissymmetry of lift.

Pilots change AOA by altering blade pitch: increasing pitch raises AOA, decreasing it lowers AOA. In powered flight, the rotor’s lift and thrust act perpendicular to the rotor disk. Hovering is the most demanding flight mode because the helicopter creates its own turbulent airflow, requiring continuous pilot corrections. The cyclic eliminates horizontal drift, the collective maintains altitude by changing blade pitch (and thus lift and drag), the throttle (or governor) controls rotor RPM, and the pedals set heading. Adjusting any one control necessitates adjustments in the others, creating a constant correction cycle.

During a steady hover, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, resulting in a balanced state. The main rotor’s thrust can be varied by changing collective pitch, which alters AOA, drag, and the engine power needed to keep rotor speed constant. Hover drag consists mainly of induced drag from lift production, with smaller contributions from blade profile drag and parasite drag of non‑lifting components.
summary.short_summary: Cyclic feathering controls rotor attitude without changing lift

topics.context:
landing gear. Throughout the rest of this discussion, the term “drag” includes induced, profile and parasite drag. An important consequence of producing thrust is torque. As discussed earlier, Newton’s Third Law states: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Therefore, as the engine turns the main rotor disk in a counterclockwise direction, the helicopter fuselage wants to turn clockwise. The amount of torque is directly related to the amount of engine power being used to turn the main rotor disk. As power changes, torque changes. To counteract this torque-induced turning tendency, an antitorque rotor or tail rotor is incorporated into most helicopter designs. A pilot can vary the amount of thrust produced by the tail rotor in relation to the amount of torque produced by the engine. As the engine supplies more power to the main rotor, the tail rotor must produce more thrust to overcome the increased torque effect. This control change is accomplished through the use of antitorque pedals (See page 3-4). **Translating Tendency (Drift)** During hovering flight, a single main rotor helicopter tends to move in the direction of tail rotor thrust. This lateral (or sideward) movement is called translating tendency. [Figure 2-27] To counteract this tendency, one or more of the following features may be used. All examples are for a counterclockwise rotating main rotor disk.
  • The main transmission is mounted at a slight angle to the left (when viewed from behind) so that the rotor mast has a built-in tilt to oppose the tail rotor thrust.
  • Flight controls can be rigged so that the rotor disk is tilted to the left slightly when the cyclic is centered. Whichever method is used, the tip-path plane is tilted slightly to the left in the hover.
  • The transmission is mounted so the rotor shaft is vertical with respect to the fuselage, the helicopter “hangs” left skid low in the hover. (The opposite is true for rotor disks turning clockwise when viewed from above.)
  • The helicopter fuselage will also be tilted when the tail rotor is below the main rotor disk and supplying antitorque thrust. The fuselage tilt is caused by the imperfect balance of the tail rotor thrust against the main rotor torque in the same plane. The helicopter tilts due to two separate forces, the main rotor disk tilt to neutralize the translating tendency and the lower tail rotor thrust below the plane of the torque action.
  • In forward flight, the tail rotor continues to push to the right, and the helicopter makes a small angle with the wind when the rotors are level and the slip ball is in the middle (See page 12-2). This is called inherent sideslip. For some larger helicopters, the vertical fin or stabilizer is often designed with the tail rotor mounted on them to correct this side slip and to eliminate some of the tilting at a hover. (By mounting the tail rotor on top of the vertical fin or pylon, the antitorque is more in line with or closer to the horizontal plane of torque, resulting in less airframe (or body) lean from the tail rotor.) Also, having the tail rotor higher off the ground reduces the risk of objects coming in contact with the blades, but at the cost of increased weight and complexity.

Figure 2-27. A tail rotor is designed to produce thrust in a direction opposite torque. The thrust produced by the tail rotor is sufficient to move the helicopter laterally.

**Pendular Action** Since the fuselage of the helicopter, with a single main rotor, is suspended from a single point and has considerable mass, it is free to oscillate either longitudinally or laterally in the same way as a pendulum. This pendular action can be exaggerated by overcontrolling; therefore, control movements should be smooth and not exaggerated. faqs.question: What causes the helicopter fuselage to want to rotate clockwise when the main rotor turns counter‑clockwise?
faqs.answer: The engine torque that turns the main rotor disk counter‑clockwise creates an equal and opposite reaction on the fuselage, making it want to rotate clockwise. The amount of this torque is directly related to the engine power used to turn the rotor.

faqs.question: How does the tail rotor (antitorque rotor) counteract the torque‑induced turning tendency?
faqs.answer: The tail rotor produces thrust opposite to the torque direction. By varying the tail‑rotor thrust with the antitorque pedals, the pilot generates enough force to balance the engine torque and keep the fuselage from rotating.

faqs.question: What is “translating tendency” (or drift) during hover?
faqs.answer: Translating tendency is the lateral movement of a single‑main‑rotor helicopter in the direction of the tail‑rotor thrust while hovering.

faqs.question: What design features are used to reduce or eliminate translating tendency?
faqs.answer: Several methods are used: • mounting the main transmission at a slight left angle so the rotor mast tilts opposite the tail‑rotor thrust; • rigging the cyclic so the rotor disk is slightly left‑tilted when centered; • mounting the transmission so the rotor shaft is vertical, causing the left skid to sit low in hover; • positioning the tail rotor higher on a vertical fin or pylon to align its thrust more with the torque plane; and • using the horizontal stabilizer to help correct inherent sideslip in forward flight.

faqs.question: Why does a helicopter sometimes tilt when the tail rotor is below the main rotor disk?
faqs.answer: When the tail rotor is below the main rotor, its thrust acts in a different vertical plane than the torque. The imperfect balance of these forces causes the fuselage to tilt, adding to the tilt created by the main‑rotor disk to neutralize translating tendency.

faqs.question: What is “inherent sideslip” in forward flight?
faqs.answer: In forward flight the tail rotor continues to push to the right, causing the helicopter to make a small angle with the wind when the rotors are level and the slip ball is centered. This small angle is called inherent sideslip.

faqs.question: What is pendular action and how can it be exaggerated?
faqs.answer: Pendular action is the oscillation of the helicopter fuselage, suspended from a single point, like a pendulum—either longitudinally or laterally. Overcontrolling the cyclic or antitorque pedals exaggerates this motion; smooth, moderate control inputs are required to keep it minimal.

faqs.question: What role does the horizontal stabilizer play in forward and rearward flight?
faqs.answer: In forward flight the horizontal stabilizer helps level the helicopter. In rearward (downwind) flight it can press the tail downward, which may cause a tail strike if the helicopter is moved rearward into the wind.

faqs.question: Why might a tail strike occur when flying rearward?
faqs.answer: When the helicopter moves rearward, the horizontal stabilizer experiences a downforce that pushes the tail down. If the aircraft is turned rearward into the wind, this downforce can make the tail strike the ground.

faqs.question: What does the statement “drag includes induced, profile and parasite drag” mean?
faqs.answer: It means that, for the purposes of the discussion, the term “drag” refers to the total aerodynamic resistance experienced by the helicopter, which is the sum of induced drag (from lift production), profile drag (from blade shape), and parasite drag (from the aircraft’s body and other non‑lifting components).

This torque is proportional to engine power and must be countered by an antitorque (tail) rotor, whose thrust is adjusted via antitorque pedals. During hover, the tail‑rotor thrust creates a lateral movement called translating tendency or drift. Designers mitigate this by tilting the transmission or rotor mast leftward, rigging the cyclic to produce a slight left tilt, or allowing the fuselage to hang low on the left skid. When the tail rotor is positioned below the main rotor, its thrust adds a vertical component that further tilts the airframe. Smooth, moderate control inputs are required to avoid exaggerated oscillations. Coning

In order for a helicopter to generate lift, the rotor blades must be turning. Rotor disk rotation drives the blades into the air, creating a relative wind component without having to move the airframe through the air as with an airplane or glider. The maximum centrifugal force generated is determined by the maximum operating rotor revolutions per minute (rpm).

faqs.question: What is rearward hover and why must it be performed with caution?

faqs.question: What causes the rotor blades to form a cone during takeoff?
faqs.answer: When lift on the blades increases, two forces act simultaneously: centrifugal force pulling the blades outward and lift pulling them upward. faqs.question: How does rotor RPM affect the coning angle of the blades?

Lower RPM reduces centrifugal force, allowing the lift‑induced upward force to dominate, which increases the coning angle. If RPM falls too low, the blades can fold up with no chance of recovery.

faqs.question: What happens if the rotor RPM drops below the minimum power‑on RPM?
faqs.answer: The centrifugal force becomes insufficient to counteract lift, causing the coning angle to become very large. At a sufficiently low RPM the rotor blades can fold upward and the helicopter may become unrecoverable.

faqs.question: What is the Coriolis Effect (law of conservation of angular momentum) as it relates to helicopters?
faqs.answer: The Coriolis Effect states that a rotating body’s angular momentum remains constant unless an external force acts on it. For a helicopter rotor, the angular momentum (moment of inertia × rotational speed) stays the same unless forces such as changes in blade radius or external torques are applied.

faqs.question: How does the conservation of angular momentum explain changes in rotor speed when blade radius changes?
faqs.answer: If the mass of the rotating blades moves closer to the rotor hub (decreasing radius), the moment of inertia decreases, so the rotor must spin faster to keep angular momentum constant. Conversely, moving mass outward increases the moment of inertia and reduces rotor speed.

faqs.question: What example is used to illustrate the conservation of angular momentum?
faqs.answer: A figure skater spinning on ice is used as an example: when the skater pulls arms and a leg inward, the moment of inertia decreases and the spin rate increases, demonstrating conservation of angular momentum.

faqs.question: What are the main forces acting on rotor blades during takeoff?
faqs.answer: The two major forces are centrifugal force, which pulls the blades outward from the hub, and lift, which pulls the blades upward. Their combined effect creates the conical shape of the rotor disk during takeoff.

summary.long_summary:
The passage explains three aerodynamic and mechanical concepts relevant to helicopter flight. First, pendular action occurs because the helicopter’s fuselage is suspended from a single point at the rotor mast head, causing the body to behave like a pendulum. Diagrams (Figure 2‑28) illustrate how the rotor disk tilts backward in rearward flight, forward in forward flight, and remains flat in a calm hover. Rearward hover into wind demands caution to avoid tail strikes. The amount of pendular motion differs between rotor systems: a fully articulated system’s hard‑blade offset transfers centrifugal forces to the fuselage, making the fuselage follow the rotor attitude, whereas a semirigid system acts as a true pendulum, requiring thrust‑generated moments to control fuselage orientation, a factor later relevant to mast‑bumping.

Second, coning describes the upward‑tilted, cone‑shaped rotor disk that forms when lift and centrifugal force act simultaneously on the blades. Centrifugal force, generated by rotor RPM, pulls blades outward, giving them rigidity. As lift increases (e.g., during takeoff), the upward lift combines with outward centrifugal force, causing the blades to assume a conical path (Figure 2‑29). If RPM falls below the minimum power‑on value, centrifugal force diminishes, the coning angle enlarges, and blades can fold, leading to loss of control.

Third, the Coriolis effect—more precisely, the law of conservation of angular momentum—is introduced. It states that a rotating body maintains its angular momentum unless acted upon by an external torque. Angular momentum equals the moment of inertia (mass × radius²) multiplied by rotational speed. Changing the radius of rotating mass (as a skater pulls arms inward) alters the moment of inertia, causing the rotation speed to increase proportionally, illustrating the principle. This concept underlies rotor dynamics in helicopters, where blade mass distribution and rotational speed affect the forces experienced during flight.

Overall, the text links pendular behavior, blade coning, and angular momentum conservation to explain how rotor design and flight conditions influence helicopter stability and control.

Gyroscopic precession is the resultant action or deflection of a spinning object when a force is applied to this object. This action occurs approximately 90° in the direction of rotation from the point where the force is applied (or 90° later in the rotation cycle). The blade with the increased angle of incidence tends to flap up; the blade with the decreased angle of incidence tends to flap down. Decreasing the pitch causes the helicopter to descend. In a no-wind condition in which lift and thrust are less than weight and drag, the helicopter descends vertically. If lift and thrust are greater than weight and drag, the helicopter ascends vertically.
